Question

When did this outbreak start, or when was the pathogen introduced?

Estimate when a group of cases began, or when a lineage arrived, by dating its common ancestor with a molecular clock.

Dating relies on collection dates and on mutations accumulating at a measurable rate. Check for temporal signal before interpreting any date, for example with a root-to-tip regression.

Which protocol to use

Choose the group your pathogen belongs to.

If the pathogen is Viruses

  1. Viral phylogenomic surveillance

In the phylogenetic inference step, select maximum likelihood and then time-scaled phylogeny. Choose Bayesian phylogeny instead when you need credible intervals on dates or estimates of epidemic growth.

If the pathogen is Bacteria

  1. Bacterial phylogenomic surveillance

In the phylogenetic inference step, add time-scaled phylogeny. Filter recombination first, and check for temporal signal before trusting dates.

If the pathogen is Fungi

  1. Fungal phylogenomic surveillance

In the phylogenetic inference step, add time-scaled phylogeny. Many fungi accumulate mutations slowly, so samples collected over a short period may not carry enough temporal signal to date events.
